The paper derives transparency conditions where μ_c = μ_0 for TM polarization and ε_c = ε_0 for TE polarization
Resonance conditions are derived as μ_c = μ_0 for TM polarization and ε_c = ε_0 for TE polarization
The analysis assumes sub-wavelength limit conditions where ka << 1 and k_0a << 1
For TM polarization transparency, MNG and DPS materials are required
For TE polarization transparency, DPS or ENG materials are required
For TM polarization resonance (maximum RCS), MNG and DNG materials are used
For TE polarization resonance, ENG and DNG materials are used
The cylinder analyzed has infinite length with radius 'a'
Oblique incidence with both TM and TE polarizations are investigated
The normalized bistatic echo width is calculated using large argument approximations of Hankel's and Bessel's functions
Under transparency conditions, maximum RCS occurs at incident direction (φ=0°) and backscattering direction (φ=180°)
Under resonance conditions, minimum RCS occurs at approximately φ=90°
Backscattering increases when incident wavelength matches inner wavelength of scatterers
Dielectric metamaterials eliminate metallic losses compared to resonant metallic elements
The paper uses MATLAB simulation for numerical validation of analytical results
Transparency conditions are less sensitive to ohmic losses than resonance conditions
ENG materials show high sensitivity to ohmic losses near resonance
Metallic metamaterial structures suffer from narrow bandwidth resonance
The scattering coefficients c_n^TM and c_n^TE are derived from boundary conditions at the cylinder surface
Tangential components of electric and magnetic fields must be continuous at the boundary
The incident electric field is expressed using cylindrical wave function expansions
Phase matching requires the propagation constant k_z to be the same in free space and metamaterial medium
Dielectric metamaterials are preferable for fabrication from RF to optical frequency ranges
The paper demonstrates dependency of RCS on both incidence and backscattering directions
Electric and magnetic dipole moments are fundamental to designing metamaterials with desired behavior
